newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says hoped for much more from EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says hoped for much more from EU summit.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Wednesday he had hoped for much more from a European Union summit in Amsterdam and described the progress on some key areas in a watered-down new treaty as too timid.
EU leaders worked into the early hours to thrash out an updated version of the 15-nation bloc's key treaty, but even the Dutch presidency admitted the final text was modest.

The summit "is not below our expectations because we all know the European situation. Certainly it is below our hopes because we thought we could give fresh impetus to the European spirit," Prodi told reporters in Rome after his return.
"We had aimed for a radical strengthening of common foreign and defence policy. In these two areas, we took some steps forward but they were timid," Prodi said.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters in Amsterdam at the end of the intensive two-day summit that the treaty had been scaled down, but was not a fudge and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok insisted that its substance was sound.
The treaty, drafted after 15 months of preparatory negotiations, includes an employment chapter and closer cooperation on asylum, immigration and crime-busting.

But it put off changes to the internal balance of power until new members join early next century and failed to resolve a split between EU leaders over whether to integrate the Western European Union (WEU) into the bloc.
Prodi said said some important goals had nevertheless been reached. "We can proceed with enlargement and the treaty has tackled some of the problems of fundamental importance...

"But it only touched marginally on the most important elements -- the new Europe cannot be run with the unanimous votes of all countries. We need to move to majority voting and this only happened in few cases."

Despite the disappointment over the new treaty, which was to have paved the way for the challenges of admitting up to 12 new members, Italy took home renewed hopes of joining a planned single currency, the euro, in 1999.

The deal, which defused a Franco-German row by adding a resolution on fighting unemployment to a stability pact on budgetary rigour designed to keep the euro strong, sent Italian bonds to a new high on Tuesday and buoyed stocks and the lira.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told the financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore that the euro would be "broad and strong".
"A currency limited to the mark and three or four other countries from the mark area, with maybe just France as a screen to avoid too many criticisms, isn't the euro we want."
Dini told reporters that Italy would meet tough criteria in 1997 for states that aspire to join the euro and Prodi said it would not need any flexible interpretations to make the grade.
Prodi has pushed through nearly 100 trillion lire ($59 billion) of deficit cuts since he took office in May 1996 in a race to qualify Italy for membership from the start.
